title: The F1 Fantasy Strategist on Las Vegas and Qatar
excerpt:
Formula 1 opens the final triple header of 2026 with two night races in eight days, and each weekend asks a different question of your F1 Fantasy line-up.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit rewards straight-line efficiency and quick tyre warm-up in cold conditions, with the heavy braking zones around the circuit offering the best overtaking opportunities of the weekend. The Lusail International Circuit then flips the test, its relentless high-speed corners punishing tyres and placing the emphasis firmly on Qualifying.

Planning your approach across both weekends together, rather than one at a time, can give players an edge. With two deadlines inside eight days, retaining enough cost-cap flexibility to react will position the best F1 Fantasy line-ups for the closing stretch of the season.

There’s also one final mini-league of the season to consider, the Williams Mini-League, which concludes in Las Vegas and is your last chance to play for signed Williams prizes and merchandise. The winner will receive an official team cap signed by Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, with more details below.

It is never too late to join the free-to-play game and compete for great prizes on offer every race week. New players simply need to select five drivers and two constructors within the starting cost cap of $100 million.

If you need a reminder of all the action from Sao Paulo to help you choose your lineup, watch the highlights below. Remember to lock in your teams before Qualifying begins in Las Vegas at 2000 local time (0400 UTC on Saturday), and again in Lusail at 2100 local time (1800 UTC).

Global League update

P1 leads the Global League on 5,819 points, built on a Red Bull and Ferrari constructor pairing with Max Verstappen taking the 2x Boost.

P2 closed the gap with a well-timed No Negative chip in Brazil, clearing the weekend’s negative scores, and like the leader they ran Verstappen on the 2x Boost with Isack Hadjar and a Ferrari driver alongside.

P3 rounds out the top three, and the common thread is proactive 2x Boost and constructor management: all three backed Verstappen for the 2x Boost, a call worth 130 points, and each ran a Ferrari driver on the way to 345 points or more in Brazil, none of them carrying a Mercedes asset.

F1 Fantasy Strategist watchlist

Our F1 Fantasy Strategist evaluates seven in-game assets below and reviews potential chip strategies to help you challenge for the top step in F1 Fantasy’s global leaderboard.

Max Verstappen ($29.1m)

Max Verstappen has collected the Driver of the Day award in six of his last seven outings, worth 10 fantasy points each time, and he leads the grid with 8.3 overtakes per race across the last three weekends.

That form produced 65 fantasy points in Brazil, where he climbed from 21st to second, and he heads to Las Vegas as the winner in 2023 and 2025 before a Qatar Grand Prix he has won three years running.

Lando Norris ($26.0m)

Lando Norris secured his third win of the season in Brazil, converting pole position into victory for a 36-point fantasy return and his best score since the summer break.

He crossed the line second in Las Vegas last year before a post-race disqualification, and he has finished in the top four in two of the last three Qatar Grands Prix.

Liam Lawson ($11.7m)

Liam Lawson has four double-digit hauls in his last five race weekends, including 27 fantasy points in Mexico, and he qualified third at Interlagos last time out.

The Kiwi is the second-best value driver on the grid between Singapore and Brazil, returning 1.5 points per $1 million spent and arrives at a track that rewards consistency and reliability.

Carlos Sainz ($7.8m)

Carlos Sainz has averaged 6.7 fantasy points per race from Baku onwards, though Las Vegas has consistently brought out his best.

The Spaniard has finished in the top six on all three visits to the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, taking sixth and third for Ferrari before fifth for Williams last season.

Nico Hulkenberg ($7.2m)

Nico Hulkenberg has made 5.9 overtakes per race from Madrid onwards, the most of any driver on the grid, and started on the second row in Brazil.

The German has also finished in the points on his last two visits to Las Vegas – another good omen for a fantastic fantasy asset this season.

Other drivers to monitor: George Russell, Oscar Piastri

Mercedes ($34.0m)

Mercedes wrapped up the Drivers’ and Teams’ Championships across the last two races, and their average of 77.7 fantasy points per race is the highest of any constructor throughout the season.

They also lead all constructors for fastest pit stop, Qualifying teamwork and fastest lap points per race, which has made them the set-and-forget pick of 2026.

McLaren ($33.3m)

McLaren have scored 168 fantasy points across the two US-based races of 2026 so far, an average of 84.0 that compares with 49.3 across the season.

The Woking-based team arrive in Las Vegas having posted 63 points in Brazil, their best return since the Italian Grand Prix.

Other constructors to monitor: Red Bull, Racing Bulls

Chip strategy – Final Fix

The Final Fix allows you to replace one driver in your line-up after the team lock deadline has passed and before the Grand Prix begins, provided you have the budget to afford the replacement.

Las Vegas averages 108 overtakes across the last three seasons and should provide plenty of passing through the three straight-mode zones around the circuit, whereas Lusail is one of the harder venues on the calendar to overtake at.

Focus the chip on the potential for grid penalties in Las Vegas, where Qualifying runs a full day before the race and leaves time to react if one of your drivers is moved down the order, with three practice sessions beforehand to inform the call.

Featured leagues and upcoming mini-leagues

This is your last chance to join the Williams Mini-League, which concludes at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. Build your ultimate team, compete against fellow fans and put your F1 knowledge to the test for the chance to win signed Williams prizes and merchandise.

First place wins an official team cap signed by Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon. With the league decided in Las Vegas, a Final Fix played that weekend counts towards your mini-league score as well as the Global League.

Keep your eyes peeled for exciting mini-leagues opening later in the F1 Fantasy season, providing you with even more opportunities to play and win.

As always, be sure to keep a close eye on the practice sessions to help guide your decisions for drivers and teams in the lead up to the team lock deadline.

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads towards its closing stages this weekend as the Las Vegas Grand Prix kicks off the final triple header on the calendar.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Thursday, November 19, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Friday, November 20, and the Grand Prix itself on Saturday, November 21.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 2023

Track Length – 6.201km

Lap record – 1m 33.365s, Max Verstappen, Red Bull, 2025

Most pole positions – Charles Leclerc, George Russell and Lando Norris (1)

Most wins – Max Verstappen (2)

Trivia – F1 previously staged two races in Las Vegas in the early 1980s under the Caesars Palace Grand Prix moniker

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 160 metres

Safety Car probability – 33%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 67%*

Pit stop time loss – 19.96 seconds (including 2.5s stop)

*From the previous three races in Las Vegas

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: The track comprises long straights and slower corners. The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.

Turn 6 into 7 is one of the toughest braking zones, accelerating through a long left-hander before hitting the brakes for 7 – it’ll be easy to lock the inside front there.

Turn 12 is also crucial as it punctuates two long straights. Finding the balance between braking well and preparing the exit is tough, and mistakes here are punishing.

Having good braking ability and traction will be the key and, in general, corner exits will be crucial onto the long straights.

Everything you need to know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit

Las Vegas GP polesitters

2025 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)

2023 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

Las Vegas GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Tyre and strategy insight

“Tyre loads are not particularly high, with the exception of the middle sector, which features several high-speed corners,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “Graining could once again make an appearance due to the low grip levels and cool temperatures, as seen in previous editions of the race. In this case, degradation would be primarily mechanical in nature.

“Another factor to monitor will be brake lock-ups. The long straights end in demanding braking zones, where the risk of flat spots can become significant in both Qualifying and the race. Drivers will therefore need to avoid locking the front tyres at the most critical points of the circuit in order not to compromise a set of tyres.

“On paper, the fastest strategy is likely to be a one-stop race, with all three compounds potentially playing a role. Even the C5, which in its current specification has demonstrated good versatility, could represent a valid option for a race stint.

“The characteristics of this circuit also reduce the effectiveness of the traditional undercut strategy. Following a pit stop, tyres tend to lose temperature quickly along the long section between the pit-exit and the more demanding parts of the lap, reducing the advantage normally associated with fresh tyres.

“Last year's edition was affected by rain during Qualifying, resulting in extensive use of wet-weather tyres. Should similar conditions arise again, the full wet could prove particularly effective. The low temperatures and circuit layout favour a tyre with a deeper tread pattern, capable of generating and retaining temperature more easily than the intermediate.”

Current form

One week on from Kimi Antonelli securing his maiden World Championship, Mercedes sealed the 2026 constructors’ title last time out in Sao Paulo – but with a final triple header still to play out, the Silver Arrows will be keen to end their triumphant season on a positive note.

The team know what it is like to win in Las Vegas, having tasted victory with George Russell back in 2024. However, it is Max Verstappen who has the strongest record from the race’s short history after standing on the top step of the podium in 2023 and 2025.

Red Bull will be keen to add another success to that list as they look to keep McLaren at bay in the battle for P3 of the Teams’ Championship, off the back of Lando Norris’ third win of the season at Interlagos.

Ferrari, meanwhile, look safe in second place but will be hoping for a better outing in Las Vegas, with Team Principal Fred Vasseur admitting after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix that the Scuderia had been lacking performance during the weekend.

Elsewhere, Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad arrive into the event with their futures sealed – both having recently been confirmed as staying with the team in 2027 – while Haas’ new recruit Rafael Camara is set for his second F1 weekend following his debut in Brazil.

At the lower end of the standings, Cadillac remain the only squad without a point to their name as they prepare for another home event. Can the American outfit get off the mark during the final triple header?

Iconic moment

It has only been on the calendar for a few years, but the Las Vegas Grand Prix immediately provided plenty of action and drama in the inaugural 2023 race – none more so than when Charles Leclerc made a stunning last-lap pass on Sergio Perez.

title: Everything you need to know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to action with the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend. But how much do you know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit? F1.com presents your all-in-one guide…

Key Las Vegas statistics

Circuit length: 6.201km

Number of turns: 17

Number of laps: 50

Race distance: 309.958km

Lap record: 1m 33.365s – Max Verstappen (2025)

When was the Las Vegas Strip Circuit’s first Grand Prix?

Las Vegas previously staged two F1 races in the early 1980s under the name of the Caesars Palace Grand Prix – but when the City of Lights returned to the calendar in 2023, it saw the debut of the brand-new Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

Located in the heart of the city, the 17-turn street circuit sweeps past iconic sights such as the Caesars Palace, the Bellagio and the Venetian.

Three years on from launching with a memorable maiden Grand Prix in 2023, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit will host its fourth Formula 1 event this year.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

With average speeds similar to Monza – the famed Italian track known as the ‘Temple of Speed’ – the Las Vegas Strip Circuit provides plenty of opportunities for action and overtaking.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, says: “The track comprises long straights and slower corners.

“The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.

“Turn 6 into 7 is one of the toughest braking zones, accelerating through a long left-hander before hitting the brakes for 7 – it’ll be easy to lock the inside front there.

“Turn 12 is also crucial as it punctuates two long straights. Finding the balance between braking well and preparing the exit is tough, and mistakes here are punishing.

“Having good braking ability and traction will be the key and, in general, corner exits will be crucial onto the long straights.”

The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.Jolyon Palmer

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

At the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, there are three designated Straight Mode zones: the first is situated on the run between Turns 4 and 5, followed by the long section between Turns 12 and 14, and a final zone between Turns 16 and 17.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

The Overtake Detection marker here comes just out of Turn 16, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the straight towards Turn 17.

Five fun facts about the Las Vegas Grand Prix

The Las Vegas Grand Prix is held on a Saturday, marking a change from the usual weekend format

Max Verstappen has the best record so far at the event, having won the inaugural race in 2023 before scoring another victory in 2025 as well as setting a new lap record

The race is the only one on the calendar where McLaren have raced more than three times and never finished in the top five, with both cars disqualified in 2025 due to technical infringements

A different driver has claimed pole position at every Las Vegas Grand Prix to date – Charles Leclerc was the first to do so in 2023, followed by George Russell and Lando Norris

Las Vegas became the third race on the calendar to be held in the United States when it arrived in 2023, joining Miami and Austin

title: Camara offers update on plans for final races of 2026
excerpt:
Rafael Camara is preparing for his second Formula 1 appearance with Haas at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, but a decision is yet to be reached on whether he will contest the final two rounds of the season.

Camara believes he will be better prepared for his second F1 outing after an intense debut in Sao Paulo, while admitting his plans for the final two rounds of the season remain undecided.

The 21-year-old Brazilian made his F1 debut at Interlagos following Esteban Ocon's departure from Haas, navigating challenging weather conditions before finishing 20th in his first Grand Prix.

Having been confirmed for another appearance alongside team mate Ollie Bearman in Las Vegas, Camara is hoping to build on the lessons learned in Brazil as he tackles another unfamiliar circuit.

"It was a very intense weekend, but there was a lot to learn, and it will be very useful this weekend," he said. "I'm excited to race here. Obviously, it will be my first time in Vegas, so I'm trying to prepare in the best way."

Unlike his last-minute call-up in Brazil, Camara has had more time to familiarise himself with the demands of a Grand Prix weekend, leaving him feeling more at ease ahead of his second outing.

"Mentally, it will be easier because I've had more time to prepare and everything feels a bit more normal," he explained. "Having already experienced some things in Brazil, I'm calmer and know a bit more about what to expect. I think it's just maybe thinking less and doing the driving more."

While Camara is confirmed to race for Haas in 2027, he admitted a decision is yet to be made on whether he will contest the final two Grands Prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi or return to Formula 2.

"That is a good question, even to myself," he admitted. "It will be tricky to decide, but there's still a lot to happen. I'm just focused on finishing this weekend in a good way, and then we'll see what happens for the next two races."

The Brazilian added that discussions with his team would follow the Las Vegas weekend, with both options appealing to him.

"Both would be very important to me, but I still need to discuss with my team what we'll do for the next races," he said. "I would be happy with either."

Camara also spoke positively about his relationship with Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu, revealing that the pair had discussed his debut and the areas where he could improve.

"Overall, on this first weekend, he didn't complain about anything, so that was good," he said. "On Sunday, there were some things I would have expected to do better. But overall, it was a good weekend and very positive."

title: Piastri opens up on decision to split with management team
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has explained why he and his management team, led by Mark and Ann Webber, mutually agreed to part ways, with the Australian believing the time was right for a new chapter in his career.

The decision was announced following the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, bringing an end to a partnership that began in 2019 and helped Piastri secure his Formula 1 debut with McLaren in 2023.

Speaking to the media in Las Vegas, Piastri reflected on the contribution the Webbers had made to his career, explaining that both parties had reached a point where pursuing separate paths felt like the right decision.

"We were just getting to a stage in our collaboration where it was better for us to go on our separate paths," he said.

"Mark and Ann contributed so much to my career, both in placing me where I am today and the management of everything behind the scenes that nobody ever really sees. It felt like the time was right for something new."

The Webbers had already reduced their trackside involvement during the 2026 season, with Piastri's former PREMA race engineer Pedro Matos and mental coach Emma Murray taking on greater roles within his close team.

Asked whether a different management structure could benefit his performances, Piastri reiterated his appreciation for the support he had received throughout his junior career and first four seasons in F1.

"Mark played a massive part in my career, both Mark and Ann, at the end of my junior career, setting me up in Formula 1 and guiding me through those first few years," he added. "The impact they've had on my career has been enormous, and I think now it feels like the right time for us both to go on our separate adventures.

"I think having the structure around you is an important thing, and it has looked a bit different this year already and will look a bit different again in the future, probably. But they played a big part in where my career is today, so I'm very, very grateful for everything they did."

While Piastri looks ahead to a new chapter off the track, his immediate focus remains on maximising his results in the final three rounds of the 2026 season, beginning with a challenging weekend in Las Vegas.

The McLaren driver will serve a 10-place grid penalty after taking a new internal combustion engine, although the team are also introducing further aerodynamic upgrades, including a new floor

"Vegas is always unique as a weekend, and as an event," the Australian driver explained when asked about how he plans to approach the race.

"We're going to be starting a little further behind, no matter where we qualify, so it's just trying to maximise what we can. We don't know exactly where we're going to sit with things. Hopefully, the new engine is going to help out a little bit, but there's obviously going to be some spots to make up."

Despite some frustrating results in recent rounds, Piastri believes his feeling with the MCL40 has improved, particularly in Malaysia, Singapore, Baku and Brazil. The Australian pointed to his race pace at Interlagos as an encouraging sign, even if his qualifying performance prevented him from fully capitalising on that potential.

"I felt like through Malaysia, Singapore and Baku, and then Brazil as well, the results weren't always what they could have been, but the feeling in the car was definitely an improvement," he explained. "In Brazil, Qualifying was a shame because the pace I had on Sunday was the strongest that it's been for a while.

"That's the big positive. It's just about trying to convert that potential now into results."

title: 'I want to fight for the victory' in Las Vegas – Russell
excerpt:
George Russell has stated he wants "to fight for the victory and I think we can do it" in this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, having decided against taking a new turbo for his Mercedes.

The German manufacturer enters this weekend having clinched the Constructors' Championship last time out in Brazil, while Kimi Antonelli became the youngest drivers' champion at the previous round in Mexico.

Even with the pressure somewhat off the team for the remaining three rounds, a new turbo is set to be introduced with all eyes firmly fixed on finding greater performance for 2027.

Speaking on Wednesday's media day in Las Vegas, Russell stated he would not be taking the new part to avoid any grid penalty, having been given the choice himself by the team.

"I think with the performance benefit it brings, it's not huge. It's just a step in the direction as a team we want to take," he said.

"We're lucky with Mercedes that there's eight drivers running the power unit. I think five or six of them are taking the turbo, the two or three who aren't, including myself, is just because it would mean a back of grid penalty and Vegas is a track I've gone well at in the past, I enjoy it here.

"The decision I was very much involved in, they said 'if you want to take it, you can take it, if you don't, you don't'. I was happy not to because I want to fight for the victory and I think we can do it, with or without it."

Russell claimed victory in Las Vegas in 2024 and finished second last year, with the Briton hopeful of another strong result this season.

Russell currently sits third in the drivers' standings, 17 points behind Max Verstappen, but admits that finding performance over the remaining races is his main priority.

"For me what's more important is just to have some strong weekends," said Russell when asked about trying to reach P2 in the standings.

"And that doesn't necessarily just mean the result, it just means from FP1 through the weekend, showing good performances. This season it's been so up and down, even during my strong weekends, other than Baku, sometimes it hasn't been every lap of the weekend.

"That's the most important to me. Of course I'd love to finish as high as possible but that's the most important."

Team mate Antonelli stated that "we don't expect any major performance gain from" the new turbo, but that it will help more with reliability and driveability.

The new World Champion also admitted that he will try and aid Russell in his bid to finish P2 in the championship.

"On my side, first of all, I'll try to do my best and try to win as much as possible," said the Italian.

"But if there is an occasion where I need to eventually help, I'll do it for sure. I'll be a team player.

"But the main focus now is to try to win as much as possible, try to win the remaining races and finish on a high, and carry the momentum into 2027."

title: Verstappen explains his only goal for the rest of 2026
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted that securing third place in the Teams’ Championship for Red Bull remains his only goal for the remainder of the 2026 season, with the Dutchman stating that the squad can be “very proud” of their progress following their earlier struggles.

The campaign got off to a tricky start for the Milton Keynes-based outfit, who slipped behind their rivals at the front of the pack in the opening stages.

There were steps forward as the championship progressed, however, with Verstappen securing three victories in the second half of the season, climbing to P2 in the drivers’ standings and finishing on the podium in every race since Monza.

When quizzed on how much it would mean to secure that position by the end of the campaign, Verstappen responded: “I only care about staying in P3 with the team. That's the goal of the team, and of course that becomes my goal.

“But for me, I don't have any satisfaction in being second or third or P4 because that's not what you're here for. Once you have won championships, you probably just don't really care, right? Because it doesn't get remembered anyway, being in that place. At least not for me.

“But for sure, for us this season, I think we can be very proud of the progression that we made as a team. I think that's way more important than where we finish in the Drivers' Championship, to be honest.”

In terms of whether Red Bull’s progression through 2026 provides encouragement for next season, the four-time World Champion admitted that, while it is “definitely more promising”, there is still work to be done.

“We also know that we need a lot of improvements for next year to be able to put up a fight up front,” Verstappen explained. “That's what we'll work on.

“We still have a lot of things that we want to do better with this car, and also things that I think we have learned for next year. Time will tell, of course, if it's going to be good enough.”

For now Verstappen’s focus is on this weekend’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, an event that he has previously won on two occasions.

Pushed on how confident he is feeling about his prospects this time out off the back of this record – along with the eight consecutive podiums he has achieved during the second half of the season – the Red Bull driver said: “It's always very hard to know because the teams already in the last few rounds have been very close, and it's just attention to detail that can make the difference on a weekend.

“Especially with it being very cold here, trying to fire up the tyres in the right window is going to be very hard. Every single year, it's a challenge to get that right.”

title: Hamilton identifies 'main focus' ahead of Las Vegas
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc have stressed the importance of finishing the 2026 season strongly as Ferrari look to bounce back from a challenging Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the team focused on securing P2 in the Constructors' Championship and gathering valuable information ahead of next year.

Ferrari arrive in Las Vegas after Leclerc and Hamilton finished eighth and ninth respectively in Brazil, but Hamilton remains determined to deliver a result that would mean a great deal to those working behind the scenes at Maranello.

"The Constructors' Championship is the main focus," Hamilton said during media day in Las Vegas. "The main focus is making sure we solidify second in the Constructors' for the team, because that's something that means a huge amount to everyone back at the factory, but especially to me also.

"That's what we're working towards and then, if we're able to do well and keep in the battle for these last few races, maybe we can climb back up from fourth and hopefully be in the top three."

Looking ahead to 2027, Hamilton explained that the remaining three races would also offer opportunities to experiment with different setups and gather data, despite Ferrari having no new components available to test.

"This is a really important period of time," he explained. "We don't have any new components to test, but this is definitely a really important data point for us to understand and make some changes setup-wise, and try some things that we can potentially use to see if everything's working.

"There's some big changes for next year. But otherwise, right now we also have the focus on trying to make sure we maintain second in the Constructors' Championship. That's the focus."

Leclerc echoed his team mate's desire to finish the campaign positively, explaining that maintaining momentum heading into the winter break would be important for morale within Ferrari, while admitting that he is more concerned with securing further victories than his final Drivers' Championship position.

"My main focus at the moment is to try and win races, and the natural result of winning races will hopefully be second place in the Drivers' Championship," he said.

"I just want to finish the season on a high, for sure, in order to keep that good momentum. It's always important to finish the season on a high, particularly because the winter break is quite long, and for the motivation of everyone, it would be nice."

However, the Monegasque driver acknowledged that Ferrari could face another challenging weekend in Las Vegas, with cold temperatures and the circuit's long straights presenting particular concerns following the team's struggles with tyre warm-up in Brazil.

"We don't have any quick fixes, otherwise we would have put them on the car a long time ago," Leclerc admitted.

"There are things we cannot change now, and there are things that we can control and put our focus on. And that is the tyre warm-up, for example, that will be quite critical.

"If we do a very good job on that, I think it can outweigh maybe the disadvantage that we have power unit-wise. I remain hopeful, but it's going to be a big challenge for us."

title: Norris assesses McLaren's turnaround ahead of Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
Lando Norris believes that McLaren have finally reached a point "where we can almost stop playing catch up", after the team took victory at the most recent race in Brazil.

Norris came out on top of a wet-dry-wet affair in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix to deliver his and McLaren's third win of the season, following back-to-back wins during the summer in Hungary and the Netherlands.

The team's most recent victory comes after a difficult patch where it generally struggled to match the pace of Mercedes, Red Bull and Ferrari.

Speaking on Wednesday's media day ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend, Norris believes McLaren are now almost on par with the leading teams after a troublesome start to the 2026 campaign.

"The fact we had a run of some wins in the middle of the season, the fact we won in Brazil, we're seeing a lot of the good signs," he said.

"I would still say there are some issues that are more severe and more fundamental that we're trying to attack and improve for next season. But I think considering where we are now, I think we can still be very happy with how the season has gone.

"Of course, we always want more and the expectation for us as McLaren, as double constructors' champions over the last two seasons, it's going to be very high.

"We set our own goals very high but it was a very difficult challenge to achieve the championship last season and obviously start this season as well as we would have liked.

"I think we've caught up well, the team have done an amazing job, but we also know as happy as we are currently, that we have a lot more work to do because the fight is very tough against Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes.

"They're all doing a very good job but it's our first time where we can almost stop playing catch up in some way and step back, have a look at things, re-analyse things and assess what is good, what can we keep, and what are the things we really need to improve on."

McLaren sit fourth in the teams' standings, just 17 points behind Red Bull, who scored a double podium in Brazil with Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.

Norris stated that getting P3 by the end of the season would mean "a huge amount" to the team.

"I mean we're still fighting for everything possible. It's a lot of money for the whole team, for every individual in the team. As always there's a lot of natural pressure on me and Oscar [Piastri] to go out and perform well, to bring points back to the team and have two cars up there.

He added: "Third is a big goal for us. Obviously Max is doing a good job and Red Bull are doing a good job, Isack did a good job last weekend. Got a tough fight, but we're up for it."

title: Max Verstappen issues F1 refusal over 'invasion of privacy' concern
excerpt:
Max Verstappen says he will refuse to take part in F1's new contract with biometric tracking data company Whoop.

A new deal was announced ahead of the Las Vegas GP, where Whoop would be able to use driver biometric data in the world feed broadcast, including heart-rate data.

This would be used to chart how a driver is reacting at key stages during a grand prix or overtaking battles, with drivers required to give their permission for their own data to be used.

However, four-time drivers' champion Verstappen has declared that he will not be a part of the deal and share his private data.

"I won't be involved," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365.

"I don't use any device for my training; I don't use anything because, first of all, I don't like to be tracked, and I know when I am tired.

"If people want to, if drivers want it, then sure, but for me, it is not something that I like and also not what I want people to see."

When it was then put to Verstappen that it would be an invasion of his privacy, the Dutchman agreed.

"Yeah," he began.

"People don't need to know my heart rate. I also don't want to know my heart rate.

"I know when it is high, and I know when it is low.

"For me, it is definitely a privacy thing, but at the same time, as I said, I don't use it privately, even for training."

title: Fernando Alonso makes F1 retirement decision ahead of looming V8 engine return
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has declared that he will not be racing in F1 when V8 engines make their return, possibly in 2030.

Talks were held earlier this week between the FIA, F1, teams, and power unit manufacturers over dropping the turbo hybrids in use since 2014 in favour of some kind of V8 machine.

The official announcement was posted by the FIA, signalling that from 2030, a 2.1L turbocharged V8 was coming, but this was quickly pulled for mysterious reasons.

Alonso, who was weighing up retirement at the end of 2026 before deciding ultimately to stay on for his 24th F1 season in 2027, has now declared that he will not be on the grid in 2030, when FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem would like to see V8s return.

Alonso has been one of the fiercest critics of the 2026 engine regulations, decrying the effect the 50:50 power output split between the ICE and batteries has had on the cars, and leading him to brand fast corners as "charging stations" for the car.

"I will not be around for the new V8, 100%," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365.

"[I have] surprised myself [in the past], but not this time. When I stop, it will be the moment to try different things.

"It is a long way ahead, but I think it will be enough.

"It is frustrating that we did not have V8s in 2014 already.

"From 2014 to 2030 or 2031, it is 16 or 17 years of pure racing lost."

Should Alonso race in F1 2030, he would turn 49 years old during the season, and would become the first F1 driver to race at that age in a world championship grand prix since Pierro Taruffi at the 1956 Italian GP.

[Article continues below]

title: Oliver Bearman voices disappointment at 'strange' Haas F1 contract delay
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman has voiced considerable "disappointment" at the delay in agreeing a new contract to stay at Haas in 2027.

Fresh terms for Bearman to continue into a third season with the team in 2027 were expected to be a formality, with the 21-year-old expected to formally become the team leader after Esteban Ocon's exit and Rafael Camara's promotion.

Warm words were given by team boss Ayao Komatsu, indicating it would just be a matter of time before the announcement was made public, but now, with just three rounds to go in the 2026 season, Bearman still has not signed.

The seat is now the only one vacant on the 2027 grid, with the news of Valtteri Bottas being kept on at Cadillac, with Bearman expressing his major distaste for the situation.

"There is nothing new, if I am honest, and I am quite disappointed that I am sitting here at round 21 without a contract signed for next year," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is a strange situation, but we're getting there, and all I can say is that it is a bit disappointing and obviously not ideal for a driver's confidence and things like that.

"I know that I've done a good job this year, but the fact that I don't know what I am doing next year is not ideal; I can tell you that much."

Then, when asked who he was disappointed with, Bearman simply replied: "I am not going to comment on that."

The Briton then went further in his explanation of why he was feeling disappointed.

"I am certain of what I want, and it is very clear that I'm trying to stay at Haas and that I deserve to stay at Haas, at least I feel this way," he said.

"But it is a strange situation, and I really thought we had made decent progress in the last triple-header, and maybe it doesn't seem that way, so it is a little disappointing.

"But I hope we can get to the end of this weekend and I have some good news to tell you.

"It is more going into the last few races knowing that next year is good."

Bearman then dismissed concerns that should an agreement not be reached, Ryo Hirakawa could be drafted in as a ready-made, short notice, replacement, simply saying, "No, it doesn't concern me at all."

title: Lando Norris relishing huge Red Bull F1 fight worth millions to McLaren
excerpt:
Red Bull vs McLaren will be one of the major talking points in the final three grands prix of the 2026 season.

Lando Norris insists that McLaren has a "big goal" to achieve in the remainder of the F1 season - beating Red Bull to finish third in the constructors'.

With three rounds remaining, Red Bull currently holds the advantage over the outgoing champions, with 415 points to McLaren's 398 following a resurgence in form since the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Including Baku, in the six races since, Red Bull has scored 185 points to McLaren's 92, with a 76-point advantage wiped out for a 17-point deficit.

With each position in the constructors' worth millions in prize money at the end of the season, Norris is hopeful McLaren can regain the upper hand.

"We're still fighting for everything possible, and it is a lot of money for the whole team, for every individual in the team," Norris told media, including RacingNews365.

"There is a lot of pressure on me and Oscar to go out and perform well, to bring points back to the team and to have two cars up there.

"Oscar is taking a penalty this weekend, so he is coming from the middle of the pack, but we've seen consistent results and need to make sure that we're there.

"Plenty of things can still happen, but we need two cars up there fighting for points, but third is a big goal for us.

"Max and Red Bull are doing a good job, Isack did a good job last weekend, so we've got a tough fight, but we're up for it."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Norris talks McLaren bonuses

Norris then went on to talk at length about what the additional placing in the constructors' would mean for the team members in terms of bonuses, when asked by RacingNews365.

"You always talk about points and constructor points and all these things, and it's very important, but I think you often do forget the extras, the bonuses that come with it, and not for me, but for all the members of the team," he began.

So it's a hell of a lot of money from P4 to P3, and all the team members that work every day to get their bonuses at the end of the year, so they want it just as much as anyone.

"Obviously, then it is me going out and driving, and they rely upon Oscar and me to go out and do a good job, so they can buy their kids cooler presents or whatever it might be; move into the new house or whatever it is. So it obviously means a lot.

"It means a huge amount, but my motivation is wanting to go out and do well anyway. So I don't think that changes how I approach things.

"But certainly around this part of the year, when you're fighting for that kind of constructors' difference, you think of it, and I was even speaking about it with my engineers and my team during the week, on whether I try and finish P3 in the drivers', I have to fly all the way to China [for the FIA prize gala].

"Do I want to do that, or do I not try as hard? But then they don't get their bonus. So I aim to fly to China at the end of the season. If I can finish P3 in the drivers' that will hopefully mean we've had a good end to the season, and they also get a good bonus. So that's my goal."

title: Lewis Hamilton sends 'very clear' message over Charles Leclerc battles
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton says it is "very clear" that he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc understand each other's boundaries when they race wheel to wheel, after their opening-lap clash at the Mexico City Grand Prix and the fallout that followed.

Speaking on media day ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton said he had no concerns about racing Leclerc again, despite some forthright remarks on the subject in recent weeks.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion had called for "serious talks" in Mexico, where he felt Ferrari had thrown away a one-two finish.

Hamilton had led from pole, with Leclerc passing George Russell for second on the run to Turn 1. When Leclerc challenged around the outside at Turn 4, both Ferraris ran wide. Leclerc crossed the grass and rejoined in the lead, while Max Verstappen slipped ahead of Hamilton.

Leclerc received a five-second penalty, but Hamilton argued over team radio that his team-mate still had the benefit of running in clean air.

"The stewards are basically handing Charles this win," he said. Verstappen ultimately won, with Hamilton second and Leclerc fourth.

Leclerc accepted the penalty but pointed to Hamilton's defence earlier in the lap. "I could also be unhappy with how much he pushed me off the track out of Turn 1," he said. Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur accused both drivers of a "lack of respect" for the team.

At the São Paulo Grand Prix, Hamilton said Leclerc raced his team-mates harder than other rivals, citing the Monegasque’s battles with Sebastian Vettel and Carlos Sainz.

The two drivers cleared the air at Interlagos, and when RacingNews365 asked whether he feels it will be a challenge to keep their racing clean in the future, the Briton downplayed any such concerns.

"I don't think it'll be difficult," the 106-time grand prix winner told media. "I think Charles is a great driver.

"The detail we went into about stuff like that, in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other, we understand each other's boundaries, and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

"So I don't feel that will be a problem moving forward, and I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."

title: Max Verstappen concedes key F1 engine wish is 'unrealistic' as V8s set to return
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has conceded that his wish for a naturally aspirated V10 engine in F1 is "unrealistic" as he delivered his verdict on the V8 return.

An announcement from the FIA was mysteriously pulled on Tuesday confirming the return of V8 engines to grand prix racing, with FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem hopeful this can be achieved in 2030.

Instead of the old 2.4L V8 engines which were dropped after the 2013 season, the new generation will be 2.1L turbocharged V8s, designed to give manufacturers the ability to easily adapt from the current turbo hybrids.

The adoption of the turbo is required to help keep fuel consumption down, with there being no appetite for the return of refuelling from teams given the expense and dangers involved.

Offering his verdict on what is coming, Verstappen signalled that he would favour a straight V10 engine, but understands the reasons why this is not realistic.

"No, because probably at some tracks then you are not allowed to race because it will be too loud," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if the V8 plans were what he had hoped for

'If it was up to me, I would take the turbo off, and I would get rid of it, or maybe use it as a push to pass, but not too much on the battery side.

"Fuel consumption, of course, goes up a lot without the turbo, so you wouldn't need to have a bigger fuel tank if you don't want to do refuelling in races.

"So I understand that you need to have a turbo, but if it was fully up to me, I'd go back to a V10; that sounds even better.

"But I know that is not something which is realistic, so this is good.

"For sure, it is in the right direction, but it is not confirmed yet, so there are a few things they need to agree on."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen on V8s

Reflecting on the comeback for V8s, Verstappen indicated that it was a "good choice" for F1.

"I mean for sure it is better, but I cannot tell you now what I will do after 2030," he added.

"But for the sport itself, it is a good choice."

When then asked if he thought the move was a "sign" the FIA and F1 listened to the drivers, Verstappen indicated that it was.

"It is probably a combination of maybe listening to our advice, but also realising what we have is not what we want, so it is probably a bit of a combination," he said.

title: Kimi Antonelli to be hit with grid penalty for Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli will take a five-place grid penalty for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with Mercedes set to add a sixth internal combustion engine to his pool.

Kimi Antonelli will take a five-place grid penalty at the Las Vegas Grand Prix after Mercedes confirmed a sixth internal combustion engine of the season for the Italian, marking his second change beyond the permitted limit following an earlier swap at Monza.

The penalty comes as Mercedes prepares to introduce an upgraded turbocharger on its 2026 power unit, made possible by the FIA's ADUO system.

Toto Wolff confirmed the development would arrive this weekend, but revealed it will not be fitted to both cars.

"We will have the ADUO-enabled turbo specification available from this weekend," the Mercedes team principal said.

"This is primarily about proving out the development in race-weekend conditions, with the expected performance benefit relatively small.

"We anticipate running it with Kimi, whilst with George our priority is protecting his grid position, with the performance benefit likely too limited to justify taking a grid penalty."

[Article continues below]

Turbo swap not the penalty cause

Antonelli's grid drop is not down to the new turbo itself. Mercedes can fit the revised unit to his car without incurring a penalty, as it will be the fourth turbocharger he has used this season, within the four allowed under the regulations.

It is the change of internal combustion engine, his second beyond the permitted count, that triggers the five-place drop.

Russell will continue with the previous turbocharger specification. Mercedes reasoning is tied partly to penalty management and partly to reliability concerns that have emerged on the bench with the new part, meaning the expected gain was not judged worth the risk for the Briton.

For Antonelli, who has already wrapped up the drivers' championship in Mexico City, the final three rounds of the season offer a low-risk window to validate the new component in race conditions, running it alongside a fresh engine.

The upgraded turbocharger will also be made available to Mercedes customer teams, with McLaren and Alpine both set to run it.

Technically, the unit is described as marginally smaller than its predecessor, aimed at reducing turbo lag and sharpening throttle response at low revs rather than chasing outright power.

A smaller turbine spins up more quickly, cutting the delay between driver input and compressor response, a benefit expected to be most noticeable at race starts and out of slow corners.

title: Aston Martin set to confirm comeback for axed F1 driver
excerpt:
RacingNews365 has learned that Esteban Ocon could be about to join a new F1 team - and potentially drive the car before the end of 2026.

19 November 7:50AM

Esteban Ocon, who left the Haas team over the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, could drive an F1 car again, potentially before the end of 2026, RacingNews365 has learned.

According to our sources, Ocon is understood to have reached an agreement with Aston Martin to take on the role of third driver to Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll.

The Frenchman is expected to get the opportunity to test the team’s F1 car before the end of this year, with his first outing potentially taking place during the post-season test following the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, by which time Ocon's signing is expected to be officially announced.

RacingNews365 understands that the one-time grand prix winner recently completed his seat fitting, and everything is in place for him to participate in the season-ending test.

Bringing Ocon in early would be a logical move for Aston Martin. Two-time world champion Alonso will focus on his Dakar Rally preparations after the season finale, and while Stroll would be available, having the incoming driver participate in the test offers a great opportunity to gather valuable feedback ahead of 2027.

Ocon had raced for Haas up until the Friday of the Mexico City Grand Prix, meaning he has extensive experience with a stronger, more competitive 2026 car, so putting him behind the wheel of the AMR26 could provide important direction for Aston Martin.

When approached by RacingNews365, the driver's camp declined to comment on the reports, though they did not deny them either.

A team spokesperson offered the following response when asked for comment on Wednesday of the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend.

"We are regularly approached by drivers who wish to join Aston Martin, but in keeping with our policy, we do not comment on rumour and speculation."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The Road to the New Role

Ocon left Haas like a bolt from the blue over the Mexico City weekend, departing between Friday and Saturday. The team had already announced weeks earlier that they would part ways at the end of the season.

Tensions were already running high, and on that particular Friday, the two sides reportedly had a falling-out after FP2, with Ocon immediately stood down with immediate effect, and his contract then terminated a few days later.

Haas put Ryo Hirakawa in the car for that weekend, while in Brazil, new signing Rafael Camara, who was set to replace Ocon next year, made his debut.

Since the split, the Frenchman has repeatedly emphasised that he views F1 as unfinished business and that his goal is to return as soon as possible.

For a few days, rumours suggested he might have a shot at Cadillac, but on the Wednesday of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the American squad finalised its lineup for next year by confirming Valtteri Bottas would be retained.

Ocon has not recently started discussions with Aston Martin.

As RacingNews365 reported around the Austrian Grand Prix, the Frenchman was already in talks with Lawrence Stroll’s team at that time.

On that occasion, he was still hoping for a full-time race seat, anticipating that Alonso might retire.

Since he decided to stay, the third-driver role is what remains available for Ocon. Even so, this offers a glimmer of hope: it keeps him in the mix in case the Spanish veteran, the oldest driver on the grid, decides to step away at the end of next year.

Additionally, Ocon enjoys an excellent relationship with the Stroll family, and Lance Stroll is one of his closest friends both on and off the track.

title: Charles Leclerc expresses surprise at explosive article which got F1 journalist banned
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has responded to the recent article from the Daily Mail that led to journalist Jonathan McEvoy having his media pass revoked.

The FIA elected to pull McEvoy's credentials for the final three rounds of the 2026 season after an article in which he described Leclerc as a "sneaky little b*****d" following his fight with team-mate Lewis Hamilton in Mexico City for the lead on the opening lap and the resulting fallout as Ferrari lost a likely one-two finish.

Following this article, the FIA elected to withdraw the pass to McEvoy, a long-time paddock regular with over 400 grands prix to his name, as it fell short of the expected standards.

In a follow-up to this, McEvoy then laid the blame on Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur, whom he described as a "tubby little nobody" and being "out of his depth" at the Maranello helm.

The decision has not been reversed, with McEvoy remaining banned for Las Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi, as Monegasque Leclerc responded for the first time.

"I saw the article, and I was quite surprised by the choice of words, but apart from that, I don't have much to say," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"Obviously, the sanction is not up to me, and I do believe that we are in a position where there are a lot of critics, which is completely normal.

"I think the job of a journalist is to ask not-so-nice questions and to do the not-so-nice articles as well sometimes.

"I was quite surprised by the choice of words when I saw the article, and on the sanction itself, I've got absolutely nothing to do with it.

"I don't have much to say about it, and the only thing I will say is that as Formula 1 drivers, I think we are used to not this kind of criticism, but to criticism in general and to critics.

"It is definitely the job of journalists to ask the bad questions and do some tough headlines, but I was surprised by the choice of words."

title: Oscar Piastri wades into sandpaper crisis engulfing Australian cricket
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri is hopeful that the sandpaper crisis engulfing Australian cricket will be quickly resolved.

An explosive article from former Test opener Cameron Bancroft blew apart claims from Test captain Pat Cummins that he was not aware that sandpaper had been used by Bancroft to rough up a ball to generate reverse swing during a Test series against South Africa in 2018.

This is a clear breach of the rules, with Bancroft, and then-Captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner receiving lengthy bans by Cricket Australia but all eventually returned to play Test cricket - with Smith the only one still playing in 2026.

Bancroft was largely seen as the fall guy, but did not speak until after current Test skipper Cummins held a lengthy news conference last week, responding to claims made by former Test opener Usman Khawaja in his book that the entire team knew at the time that sandpaper had been used.

Cummins has long denied any knowledge of Bancroft using sandpaper, along with his fellow fast bowlers, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, and Mitchell Marsh, who all made up the pace attack during the Cape Town Test where Bancroft was caught on TV using the yellow sandpaper.

However, Cummins' latest denial prompted Bancroft to pen a 4,000-word rebuttal, saying he was asking Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood, and Marsh for feedback on how he was using the sandpaper during the Test - thus rubbishing their claims that they had no knowledge.

Piastri is a keen cricket fan, and hosted the likes of Khawaja, Starc and spin bowler Nathan Lyon at the McLaren Technology Centre ahead of the 2025 World Test Championship final, which Australia lost, and also attended the 2025 Boxing Day Ashes Test between Australia and England, which Australia also lost.

Reflecting on the situation, which exploded into life with Bancroft's article during the third ODI in Hobart, which England won to earn a 2-1 series victory, Piastri was hopeful of a quick resolution.

"It has obviously been an interesting couple of weeks, that is for sure with what has been unfolding," Piastri told media, including RacingNews365.

"I know quite a few of the guys involved personally, so it is not really a nice thing to see it being brought back up necessarily, but it is what it is.

"Obviously I've got no knowledge, and I remember when it happened eight years ago, but I think for everyone, especially the Australian cricket community and Australia as a country, the quicker it can be dealt with, whatever that looks like, the better.

"I know myself as a sports person that the noise around certainly is not going to be helpful, so the quicker it can be resolved and put behind us, the better for everyone."

title: Valtteri Bottas explains Colton Herta 'noise' as Cadillac confirm 2027 F1 driver
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has signalled that he had no concerns about Colton Herta's attempts to secure a superlicence with the Cadillac F1 team for 2027.

Herta has recently completed three more FP1 sessions to earn the required points to push him to 40 superlicence points and thus earn the legal requirement to potentially race in F1 in 2027 - with the American having eyes on Bottas's seat alongside Sergio Perez.

However, on Wednesday, Cadillac put an end to the speculation and formally confirmed Bottas will continue for 2027, with Herta to miss out on his long-held dream of becoming an F1 driver.

Addressing the "noise" around Herta's bid for the superlicence, Bottas declared that it was "always the plan" for the team to get the former IndyCar star the licence, but that he was not required to immediately use it.

"First of all, with Colton, it was always the plan this year for the team to try and get enough points for him to get the superlicence," Bottas told media, including RacingNews365.

"Because if he misses it this year, it is going to be almost impossible to get in the future, but it doesn't mean that you need to use him immediately, as it will stay valid for several years.

"So that was always the plan, so it is all good.

"There has been a bit too much noise in the last few weeks; it has been really unnecessary, but that is why we wanted to put out an official confirmation, which I've known for a while should be the case.

"So at least we can get rid of the noise, and I can just focus on the job instead of answering questions about that kind of stuff.

"So it keeps me at peace for the future, and it is exactly what I signed up for."

[Article continues below]

Bottas on Cadillac DNFs

Turning to the recent spate of DNFs, with failures to do so in Bahrain, the United States, and Mexico City as well as a DNS in São Paulo, Bottas was clear that the team needed to eradicate its reliability woes to ensure it had a chance of scoring its first point.

"We need to finish races," he said.

"There have been way too many DNFs lately, so we need to finish, because if we don't finish, then we can't be in the fight."

title: Liam Lawson responds to Helmut Marko declaration over Racing Bulls F1 seat
excerpt:
Liam Lawson says he is "grateful" Helmut Marko is not "calling the shots" anymore over driver selection for Red Bull's two teams after his support for Nikola Tsolov.

Lawson was finally confirmed last week as keeping his Racing Bulls seat for 2027, after a stunning season in which he is comfortably leading the midfield in ninth place in the standings with 89 points to his name - the most of any non-Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull, or McLaren driver.

However, despite his strong performances, including finishing seventh in four of the last five grands prix, Lawson was under threat of losing his seat to F2 protege Nikola Tsolov.

Given that Racing Bulls has been used as a training ground for young drivers for the senior Red Bull team, former driver advisor Marko threw his weight behind the Bulgarian to partner Arvid Lindblad.

"I subscribe to a saying by [Dietrich] Mateschitz: 'We don't buy stars, we make stars'," Marko told Krone.

"We've always sought out our own drivers who are capable of winning a grand prix. With a few exceptions, it's worked.

"In keeping with that philosophy, the difficult decision between Liam Lawson and Nikola Tsolov at Racing Bulls should really go in Tsolov's favour."

Facing the media for the first time since his contract was extended for 2027, with Tsolov due to become third and reserve driver for both Red Bull and Racing Bulls, Lawson addressed both the delay in his new deal and offered his response to Marko.

"I mean, there are obviously many conversations, and I think Red Bull is a big organisation with probably a lot more people involved than in a normal situation in a normal team where you maybe have one person making the call," Lawson began when asked in the first of a two-part question by RacingNews365 why there had been any reason for the delay in his renewal.

"I feel like it doesn't feel like that, but what I can say is that Alan has been extremely supportive, and I am extremely grateful for what he has done for me this year, and he's done a great job with the team as well.

"The car has been in a really good place, so I am very thankful for how he has supported me this year and how he has been to me this year."

In the second part, Lawson addressed Marko's comments.

"I think obviously if he was calling the shots and he didn't want me in the car, then yeah, I am grateful that he is not calling the shots and I am in the car."

Lawson then confirmed that Marko had not been in contact with him since the announcement had been made.

[Article continues below]

An intense period

Lawson also spoke of the "intense few weeks" whilst talks were ongoing and how he was left a little "confused" about what more he could have done to secure the seat.

"There were a lot of conversations going on, and I don't think there was a point I felt like I was going to be dropped, but at the end of the day, with delays and it being extended every race weekend, anything can happen," he added.

"It is a sport of a lot of variables, and we had a good form of races going, and I'm obviously trying to keep that rolling as long as I could.

"But every weekend is one that can turn upside down as well, so there's a lot of conversations going in the background and me trying to do everything to extract everything every weekend and then honestly asking the question: 'What more needs to be done?'

"There wasn't anything really, so then you're just left a little confused, so yeah, just an intense few weeks overall."

title: Cadillac make crucial F1 driver announcement ahead of Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas will remain with Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season, the American team has confirmed.

The announcement gives the squad continuity as it builds on its maiden campaign on the grid. It forms part of Cadillac's long-term ambition to establish itself as a competitive force at the top of the sport.

Bottas brings considerable Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team. His feedback and leadership are set to continue supporting the squad's development across its operations in Silverstone, Indianapolis and Charlotte.

"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss also welcomed the news, with the team currently preparing for this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team," said Towriss.

"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1.

"On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Reserve and test drivers for the squad are set to be announced in due course.
